Astronomers just found 70 natural telescopes hiding in the sky.
They're called gravitational lenses: a galaxy so heavy it bends the light of galaxies far behind it.
The result looks like a glowing ring or arc wrapped around the galaxy in the middle.
Finding them is brutal. A new map of the sky holds nearly four billion objects. Nobody can scroll through that by eye.
So the team trained a neural network, a residual network, to hunt for ring-shaped patterns in the pixels.
It flagged about seventy-six candidates. But a pattern isn't proof.
So they pointed the VLT's MUSE spectrograph at each one, and measured the distances to both galaxies.
Seventy were confirmed as real lenses.
Why care? Lenses magnify the early universe, and reveal invisible dark matter by how much they bend light.
The AI didn't find the answer. It narrowed the sky, so humans could spend precious telescope time where it counts.
